posts.quote: THE BARBER LAID A BOARD ACROSS THE CHAIR ARMS FOR THE LITTLE KIDS, AND THAT WAS WHEN YOU KNEW IT WAS HAPPENING.
posts.caption: The barber had a plank of wood for the small customers, and it lived behind the tonic shelf with the extra towels. He would slide it across the arms of the big leather chair, pat it twice, and you climbed up like you were boarding a ship. From up there you could see the whole shop in the mirror, including your father pretending to read the paper and watching you the whole time. The paper cape snapped around your neck, the clippers buzzed behind your ear, and you held very still because the man had scissors. When he brushed your neck with that soft powdered brush, you felt like a brand new person who happened to be missing some hair.
posts.first: My dad took me every other Saturday, and the barber always gave me a peppermint from the same glass jar when it was over. I thought the board was the best part of the whole business. I was nearly ten before I understood it was there because I was too short.

posts.character: Cars and driving culture (the glove box)
posts.quote: THE GLOVE BOX HELD A ROAD MAP NOBODY COULD REFOLD, A TIRE GAUGE, AND A FLASHLIGHT WITH DEAD BATTERIES.
posts.caption: Every glove box in America held the same three or four things, and none of them worked quite right. The road map had been opened at a gas station in another state and never folded along its original creases again. Under it sat a tire gauge, a pencil with no point, and a flashlight that gave off a brown glow for about four seconds. Somewhere in the back there was a packet of napkins from a diner that closed years ago. The door dropped open and caught your knee every time, and you pushed it shut with a click that meant the whole mess was safe for another year.
posts.first: Our glove box also held the registration, a church bulletin from 1968, and a half roll of butterscotch candies that had melted and set into one piece. My father said it was an emergency kit. I never found out what the emergency was supposed to be.

posts.quote: Every street had one porch light that stayed on all night, and the whole block quietly agreed it was for everybody.
posts.first: Ours was the Hendersons' at the corner, a plain yellow bulb in a glass jar fixture over the steps. I could see it from my bedroom window, and it was the last thing I looked at before I fell asleep. When I was grown, they told me they had never once thought about the electric bill.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the knife grinder)
posts.quote: THE KNIFE GRINDER / A FOOT PEDAL, A SPINNING STONE, AND A BELL YOU COULD HEAR FROM THE NEXT STREET
posts.caption: He came through the neighborhood every few weeks, pushing a cart with a grinding wheel bolted to the top. The little bell on the handle was the only advertisement he needed, and by the time he reached your block the women were already out on the porches with kitchen knives. He pumped a pedal with one foot, held the blade to the wheel, and sparks flew off in a thin orange fan. A dull carving knife went in and a dangerous one came out. He charged a few cents each, folded the money into his apron, and walked on to the next street ringing his bell.
posts.first: Mom saved every dull knife in the house for weeks until she heard that bell. She would stand by the cart with her arms crossed, supervising, as if he had never sharpened a knife before. He never seemed to mind, and he always handed the bread knife back handle first.

posts.quote: MILK MONEY WENT TO SCHOOL IN A SMALL ENVELOPE, AND IT WAS YOUR WHOLE JOB NOT TO LOSE IT.
posts.caption: On Monday mornings your mother counted out the coins for the whole week and sealed them in a little brown envelope. She wrote your name on the front in pencil, in case the envelope forgot who it belonged to. You carried it in your coat pocket with your hand over it, all the way down the sidewalk. At school the teacher collected them in a cigar box and checked each name off a list. A kid who lost his milk money had a very quiet week, and everyone knew who it was.
posts.first: I lost mine exactly once, in second grade, and I found it in the lining of my mitten at recess. I have never been so relieved by forty cents. After that I carried it in my shoe.

posts.quote: THE FEED STORE SCOOP HUNG ON A CHAIN SO IT WOULD NEVER WALK OFF, AND THE WHOLE PLACE SMELLED LIKE GRAIN.
posts.caption: You smelled the feed store before the door finished closing behind you, a warm mix of oats, molasses, burlap, and leather. Sacks stood in tall stacks along the wall, stenciled with the name of a mill two counties over. A brass scale sat near the counter with a tin scoop chained to it, because everyone had learned the hard way what happens to loose scoops. Men stood around the stove with their hats on, talking about weather in numbers. You came in for fifty pounds of something and stayed twenty minutes without ever deciding to.
posts.first: My grandfather bought his chicken feed there every other Friday for thirty years. The owner knew what he wanted before he got to the counter, and they never once talked about money. They talked about rain, and the price of corn, and whose roof had gone.

posts.quote: The little radio sat on the kitchen windowsill, and it was never turned off, only turned down.
posts.first: Ours had a cracked dial and a coat hanger wired to the back for reception. It played the farm report, then the ball game, then something with violins, and my mother worked to all of it without ever looking up. When the power went out one night, the kitchen felt strangely empty, and it took us a minute to see why.

posts.quote: THE TABLE LEAF LIVED BEHIND THE HALL CLOSET ALL YEAR, AND IT ONLY CAME OUT WHEN THE WHOLE FAMILY DID.
posts.caption: Sometime in the third week of November, somebody said it was time to get the leaf. Two grown men went to the back of the hall closet, and there was always a short argument about who was holding which end. The leaf had been stored behind the winter coats since last Thanksgiving, and it came out wearing a little dust and carrying a smell of cedar. The dining table was pulled apart in the middle, and the leaf dropped in, and suddenly the room had space for the cousins. Mom came behind them with the white tablecloth and smoothed the seam, and you could feel the holiday arrive.
posts.first: We had to add the second leaf when Aunt Ruth's family drove in, and it never quite matched the first. One side was a shade darker, and nobody was allowed to mention it. I think that mismatched seam is the thing I would miss the most from those tables.

posts.character: Old jobs and skills (the shoe repairman)
posts.quote: THE SHOE REPAIRMAN / A LAST, A HANDFUL OF TINY NAILS, AND NEW HEELS BY FRIDAY
posts.caption: The little shop on the corner smelled like leather, polish, and hot glue, and the bell on the door was always a half second late. Behind the counter sat a man in a leather apron with a mouthful of tiny nails, tapping them in one after another without looking. Shoes were fixed in those days, not replaced, and every pair came back with a fresh heel and a shine. He wrote your name on a paper tag, tied it to the laces, and said Friday. On Friday the shoes were waiting on the shelf in a neat row, and the tag was still on.
posts.first: Dad had his work boots resoled so many times they were mostly repairs by the end. He carried them in under his arm like a loaf of bread. The cobbler called him by name, and I remember thinking that must be what it feels like to belong somewhere.

posts.quote: WHEN DAD WORKED NIGHTS, THERE WAS A TOWEL OVER THE BEDROOM WINDOW, AND THE WHOLE HOUSE WALKED ON SOCKS UNTIL FOUR.
posts.caption: At two in the afternoon, the house was as quiet as church. A towel was tacked over the bedroom window, and the door was shut, and Dad was asleep behind it after a night at the plant. Everyone moved at half speed, like they were carrying eggs. The cereal bowls were washed without clanking, and the radio was turned to a murmur, and the dog was told to lie down in a whisper. Around four the bedroom door finally opened, and he came out in his undershirt, squinting like a man who had been somewhere far away. That was the signal to start being a normal family again.
posts.first: I once dropped a pan lid in the kitchen at noon, and the sound went through the house like a gunshot. My mother just closed her eyes and counted to ten. Dad slept through it, or at least he let us believe he did.
